hits.name: Benjamin Bikman
hits.text:
Calling metformin a mitochondrial poison sounds dramatic, but it's an accurate description of how the most prescribed diabetes drug in the world actually lowers blood glucose. Unfortunately, the mechanism is a kind of blunt instrument.

One of metformin's best-described actions is that it inhibits complex I of the mitochondrial electron transport chain, the first step cells use to turn the fuel we eat into ATP. With complex I partly blocked, the cell makes less energy, and that energy shortfall activates AMPK and slows how much glucose the liver makes and releases into the blood. Put plainly, metformin lowers glucose largely by making cells a little worse at producing energy, and the liver and gut wall take the heaviest exposure because they pull the drug in through their transporters.

That matters most in muscle when someone is trying to get healthier through exercise, since the main benefits of training come from muscle building more and better mitochondria and becoming more sensitive to insulin.

In older adults doing 12 weeks of aerobic training, the group taking metformin lost much of the gain in mitochondrial respiration that exercise produced, and the improvement in whole-body insulin sensitivity was blunted compared with the group on placebo.

In another trial of older adults doing 14 weeks of resistance training, the people taking metformin gained less muscle mass and less thigh muscle than those taking placebo, and the usual training response in their muscle tissue was dampened.

I'm not overtly opposed to metformin, and for a sedentary person with high blood glucose it can have a place, but I see its usefulness dropping as exercise goes up, since the more someone trains, the more the drug works against the very adaptations they're working for.

I also find it bizarre that metformin gets promoted as a longevity hack, because it's hard for me to believe that a drug that compromises mitochondrial function, which is so central to healthy aging, would be the key to living longer.

For anyone using exercise to improve their metabolic health, and especially for older adults trying to hold on to muscle, it's worth knowing that metformin and exercise can pull in opposite directions inside the muscle cell.
hits.draft_en:
Prof Ben Bikman makes a point every older bloke on metformin should hear.

Metformin lowers blood sugar partly by making cells a bit worse at making energy. In older adults doing 12 weeks of aerobic training, the ones on metformin lost much of the gain in their muscle's energy output that exercise gave the placebo group. In a 14-week weights trial, the metformin group put on less muscle.

He's not saying stop it. If you're on it and you're training to hold on to your muscle, have a yarn with your doctor about it. Don't change any medication on your own.

hits.name: David Sinclair
hits.text:
Taurine is the most controversial amino in the longevity field.

Prof. Deep Dixit's latest paper in Cell shows circulating taurine actually increases with age, a possible compensatory, adaptive attempt by the body to counter inflammation. Boosting taurine levels diminishes the effects of inflammaging. 

Giving extra taurine to aged mice reduced inflammation, improved physical markers like grip strength, and lowered mortality from sepsis. The work helps reconcile previous contradicitons and academic quarrels. This new paper scores a point for the taurine team

A brief history: 

A 2023 paper in Science suggested supplementing with taurine restored youthful levels and extended the healthspan and lifespan of worms and mice, as well as the healthspan of rhesus macaque monkeys.  Blood levels of taurine were shown to decline with age in mice, monkeys, and humans. David started taking taurine.

A large-scale longitudinal study at NIH and published in Science later cast serious doubt on these claims. David stopped taking taurine. 

Today: Deep and team observed that macrophages dump up to 80% of their taurine when exposed to danger signals, not through standard cell-rupture pores  or known taurine transporters. The exact channel or mechanism letting taurine flood out of the cell is still unknown

While overall blood taurine rises with age as a compensatory response, the Dixit lab doesn't yet know why aging immune cells become prone to leaking their internal taurine stores or how to help them hold onto it

A single 4 g oral dose in eight men produced a peak blood-plasma concentration of about 0.69 mM after roughly 1.5 hours, at least 10X less than what was needed in this study for anti-inflammatory effects 

So, can oral doses in humans raise intracellular macrophage levels high enough, and safely enough, to replicate this effect? Someone should do a trial
hits.draft_en:
Taurine has gone back and forth in the longevity world, and David Sinclair just laid out the latest round.

A 2023 study said it extended life in worms and mice. A big NIH study later cast doubt on that, and Sinclair stopped taking it. Now a new Cell paper says taurine in the blood actually rises with age, maybe as the body's way of fighting inflammation, and extra taurine helped old mice.

His own catch: a normal 4 g dose in people gave blood levels at least 10 times lower than what worked in the study. So it's still mice, not men. Someone needs to run a proper human trial before anyone gets excited.

hits.name: Dr Shawn Baker 🥩
hits.text:
Low-carb diets and your thyroid: what the data actually show

For years the internet has warned that cutting carbs will “wreck your thyroid.” The claim usually rests on one lab finding: T3 often drops on a ketogenic or low-carb diet. What the studies rarely mention is that TSH stays flat or falls, free T4 holds steady or rises, and people do not develop clinical hypothyroidism.

A 2016 trial in overweight adults with Hashimoto’s tested a low-carbohydrate diet (restricted bread, pasta, fruit, and rice, free of goitrogens) for three weeks. Thyroid antibodies plummeted: antithyroid −40 %, anti-microsomal −57 %, TPO −44 %. The control group’s antibodies went up. 

Thyroid hormones themselves did not change significantly, while weight and BMI dropped.
A 2024 randomized study used MRI (Dixon-T2 imaging) to measure thyroid inflammation in Hashimoto’s patients. After six months on a low-carb diet, thyroid water content fell and both TPOAb and TgAb declined significantly. The normal-diet group showed no improvement.

In people with metabolic syndrome, a 2024 trial of time-restricted eating with or without a low-carb diet improved markers of thyroid function alongside heart-muscle enzymes. Clinical programs tracking hundreds of patients on well-formulated ketogenic diets (including Yancy et al. in type 2 diabetes) have not produced new cases of hypothyroidism. TSH remains stable while T3 adapts downward—exactly the pattern seen in fasting, not thyroid failure.

The T3 drop appears adaptive: when insulin and glucose stay low, the body needs less active thyroid hormone to clear carbohydrate. It is not the same as primary hypothyroidism, which requires a rising TSH plus symptoms.

Well-constructed low-carb eating does not damage the thyroid. In autoimmune thyroid disease it can lower the antibodies and the inflammation driving the attack. The old fear was based on incomplete lab numbers, not outcomes.

hits.name: Dr Shawn Baker 🥩
hits.text:
In the late 1990s, researchers at the University of Sheffield ran a small but tightly controlled experiment on twenty healthy young adults. Everyone started on the same familiar British-style diet—about 41 percent of calories from fat—for a full month. Then half the group quietly switched to a lower-fat pattern of 25 percent of calories from fat while total calories stayed exactly the same. The other half kept eating the original higher-fat meals.
After four weeks the difference showed up not on the scale, but on a standard mood questionnaire. Anger and hostility scores climbed in the people who had cut the fat. In the group that stayed on the higher-fat diet, those same scores drifted slightly downward. Tension and anxiety eased in the higher-fat group and stayed flat in the low-fat group. Blood cholesterol moved only modestly, and the mood shifts did not track with the lipid changes. The researchers wrote that simply dropping from 41 percent to 25 percent fat “may have adverse effects on mood.”
The finding was never a blockbuster. The sample was small, the intervention lasted only a month, and later weight-loss trials sometimes painted a more favorable picture of lower-fat diets when people were also losing weight. Still, the study remains one of the few controlled human experiments that held calories constant and watched hostility rise as dietary fat fell. It sits alongside older primate work in which monkeys on lower-fat diets became more aggressive and less affiliative.
Fat is more than calories. It is also a signal—to the gut, to hormones, and apparently, in at least some people under some conditions, to mood. When the signal is dialed down sharply and nothing else changes, the body may answer with a sharper edge. The Sheffield volunteers simply showed what that edge can look like after thirty days.
hits.draft_en:
Dr Shawn Baker dug up a 1990s Sheffield study. Twenty healthy adults ate a normal British diet, about 41% of calories from fat. Then half cut fat to 25% with calories kept the same.

After four weeks, anger and hostility scores went up in the low-fat group. In the group that kept eating fat, they drifted down.

It's a small study and he says so. But it's a reminder that food isn't just fuel. If you've gone hard on cutting fat and you're cranky all the time, it might be worth a look.

In the mid-1990s, researchers at the Minneapolis VA Medical Center set out to study what happens when people lose weight very fast. They randomized obese volunteers to one of two liquid diets: a near-zero-fat 520-calorie plan (<2 g fat per day) or a 900-calorie plan that included 30 g of fat, with one daily meal designed to trigger a full gallbladder contraction.
The trial barely got started. Within weeks, ultrasound showed new gallstones in 4 of the 6 people on the ultra-low-fat diet. None of the 7 people eating the modest 30 g of fat developed any. The difference was so stark (p = 0.021) that the investigators stopped the study early on ethical grounds. The low-fat diet produced only about half the normal gallbladder emptying; bile sat still, cholesterol crystallized, and stones formed before anyone had lost much weight.
This was not an isolated curiosity. Similar very-low-calorie, very-low-fat trials from the same era produced gallstones in roughly one-quarter to one-half of participants. The pattern was consistent: when dietary fat falls low enough that the gallbladder is rarely asked to squeeze, stasis plus cholesterol-rich bile becomes a perfect storm.
That finding landed in the middle of a much larger cultural experiment. From the late 1970s onward, official dietary guidelines steadily pushed the public toward lower fat intakes. Fat was framed as the primary dietary villain; grocery shelves filled with fat-free and low-fat products. Over the same decades, U.S. gallstone disease prevalence roughly doubled—from about 7.4% in the late 1980s to 13.9% by 2017–2020—while rates of gallbladder surgery rose in parallel.
The parallel is not proof of simple cause and effect. Obesity, insulin resistance, and rapid weight-loss cycles also climbed. Yet the mechanistic evidence is hard to ignore: the gallbladder is a muscle that needs periodic mechanical work. Extremely low-fat diets, whether temporary or habitual, deprive it of that work. The 1996 trial simply showed, in real time and under controlled conditions, what a population-scale reduction in dietary fat might have been doing more slowly for years.
Fat is not merely a calorie. For the gallbladder, it is the signal to empty. Remove the signal and the organ can quietly fill with stones.

hits.text:
Calories matter, but when it comes to hunger and satiety, not all calories are equal. A meal built mostly on carbohydrate does a weaker job of switching on the body's fullness signals than a meal built on protein or fat, even when the calories are exactly the same, and the gap is widest in people who are already insulin resistant.

One study gave people three different meals on separate days, each with the same calories but with most of the energy coming from carbohydrate, protein or fat, and then tracked the gut hormones that tell the brain whether a person has eaten enough over the next six hours. Some of the subjects were lean and insulin sensitive, while others had obesity and insulin resistance. All of them still had normal blood glucose.

GLP-1 (a satiety signal) rose more after the protein meal and the fat meal than after the carbohydrate meal, and that was true in both the lean and overweight people. In the those with insulin resistance, the fat meal also produced a bigger rise in PYY, another hormone that signals fullness, and the protein and fat meals pushed ghrelin, the main hunger hormone, down further than the carbohydrate meal did.

This helps explain why a breakfast based on carbs so often leaves a person hungry again by mid-morning, while a breakfast of eggs and meat can hold them until lunch. The body's own satiety system responds more strongly to protein and fat, and a person who is insulin resistant appears to get even less of that signal from a carb-heavy meal, which makes it harder for them to stop eating at the very point when they most need to.

If someone struggles with hunger soon after eating, it's clear that building meals around protein and fat rather than carbohydrate gives the body's natural fullness hormones a much better chance to do their job.

hits.name: Benjamin Bikman
hits.text:
Four in ten young American adults without diabetes are already insulin resistant, and nearly half of them aren't obese.

That finding comes from national health survey data on adults between 18 and 44 who had neither diabetes nor heart disease, which is the group most people assume is metabolically safe. Insulin resistance was common across a full decade of surveys, and the share stayed high from one survey cycle to the next.

The young adults with insulin resistance were already carrying more of the problems that eventually lead to heart disease and diabetes, with high blood pressure and high cholesterol each about twice as common as in their insulin-sensitive peers, along with lower levels of physical activity.

The part that matters most for how people get screened is that body weight only partly lined up with insulin resistance. A higher BMI, a larger waist and more body fat were all associated with it, but nearly half of the young adults who were insulin resistant weren't obese, which means a normal reading on the bathroom scale doesn't rule it out.

Insulin resistance also tends to hide on standard blood work. Glucose can stay normal for years because the pancreas keeps making more insulin to hold it there, so the earliest sign of trouble is often a rising fasting insulin, and that's a test most doctors don't routinely order.

For a young adult, this is the stretch of life when insulin resistance is easiest to turn around, long before glucose climbs high enough to earn a diagnosis of prediabetes or diabetes, and the researchers themselves concluded that screening for insulin resistance regardless of BMI may be needed.

If a young adult wants to know where they stand metabolically, adding a fasting insulin test to the usual glucose check gives a far clearer picture than weight or glucose alone.

Today is World Diabetes Day, and I'm working toward the day we won't need one anymore.

Make no mistake, this is not a holiday. It should be a day of embarrassment for the medical and pharmaceutical industries, which have managed diabetes for decades instead of ending it. It should be a day of reckoning for the ultra-processed food industry, which keeps feeding the epidemic. 

It should be a day of education for every patient with diabetes, who deserves to know the truth about what they eat. And it should be a day of remembrance for everyone we've lost to diabetes and its complications, people who should still be with us.

Diabetes kills far more people than the official numbers admit. Death certificates name diabetes as the main cause for about 100,000 Americans a year. But the ADA's own analysis estimated that diabetes caused about 339,000 deaths in the US in 2022, including about 179,000 from heart disease, 25,000 from stroke, and 28,000 from kidney disease. That's more than three times the official count, almost a thousand Americans every single day. Every one of them was somebody's mother, father, child, or friend.

So before you scroll on, take a moment and remember someone you've lost because of diabetes. Say their name out loud or in the comments.

Here's the world I'm working toward. Everyone knows exactly what causes type 2 diabetes. Parents know it, schools know it, and doctors teach it from the first visit. No child ever gets type 2. The only adults who still have it are the rare few who choose not to change how they eat, and even they know the door is open whenever they're ready.

It's a world where the last person with type 1 diabetes has been cured, with beta cell transplants. No more finger sticks at 3 AM, no more counting every carb just to stay safe, no more parents checking on their child through the night. Insulin pens end up in museums next to iron lungs.

On that day, November 14 won't need to be about diabetes at all. We can find something better and more joyful for this day to be.

We're not there yet. Until we are, the American Diabetes Society will keep teaching people with type 2 that they can reverse it completely without medication, and teaching people with type 1 that they can reach a normal A1C using 70-80% less insulin on a very low carb diet.

outsiders.text:
✨ Progress update:

I imported the entire catalogue of @IKEA in 3d into Interior AI after seeing someone do the same yesterday, I'll try to import more furniture brands soon to get more variety too

Anyway so now you can import your home's blueprint or do a walk through video, it then rebuilds your home, and then you can redecorate it

This is now day 4 of rebuilding Interior AI now that's the models are smart enough to do 3d stuff properly, it still looks a bit clunky and all but it's going somewhere! 😊

outsiders.name: @levelsio
outsiders.text:
Noo I asked Claude what to use 100% free and it said OBS with a circle mask on the webcam

It even made the circle mask for me 😃 https://t.co/8oP3w7ttK8 https://t.co/Fqnuo4m81r

outsiders.name: Ethan Mollick
outsiders.text:
AI is getting better faster than our measurements are

I threw together SatBench, which measures how quickly major AI benchmarks become saturated (effectively beaten). Of 173 benchmarks cited by the Labs since 2023, 63% are now saturated. Saturation is happening faster each year. https://t.co/tITFRo7w0z

outsiders.name: OpenAI
outsiders.text:
Physicist Nathaniel Craig shares how he worked with GPT-6 Astra to develop a candidate lattice definition of the Standard Model.

It’s the first post on our new science blog:
https://t.co/pLd0XmTUxD

outsiders.name: Ethan Mollick
outsiders.text:
AI slop replies, ranked by annoyingness:
6) Repeating the post
5) LLM knows more than the account should about a topic
4) Lame semi-joke
3) "X is the part I would keep/everyone misses..."
2) "As a marketer/builder/dentist, I see this in my own..."
1) Questions faking "curiosity"

outsiders.name: Ethan Mollick
outsiders.text: The traffic from agent swarms doing research is going to be quite large, they are relentless. I had Fable 5.2 reconstruct WH Auden's 1941 poetry class. It found an obscure, relevant book on the Internet Archive, which it read a line at a time by doing repeated full text searches. https://t.co/bBtxGguUuT

outsiders.name: @levelsio
outsiders.text:
What's easier than trying to build a giant furniture library?

Letting users just upload their own furniture they want as a photo and then turn it into a 3d object in less than 30 seconds with an image-to-3d model ofcourse! https://t.co/n878FlRw7Z https://t.co/XDStwhZBuZ

outsiders.name: swyx
outsiders.text: obviously correct, we are so suboptimal in AI UX rn it is crazy esp given existence of models too cheap to meter https://t.co/6S0eWejPXK

outsiders.name: Aravind Srinivas
outsiders.text: A week later, it’s 11x more agent hours per week from Teammate. Growing more than 50% week over week (was 7x last week). The number of employees getting an extra workday (8+ hours) and extra work week (40+ hours) from Teammate has more than tripled in a week since September. https://t.co/nAPbK4OGUO https://t.co/xMVB6hoPHq

outsiders.name: Ethan Mollick
outsiders.text: Not having a good AI model powering your central home device will be a growing liability. You see the difference when you have a central PC with Codex/Code/OpenClaw and you try to use Siri or Alexa. Frontier models act like the household computer from sci-fi & are more intuitive.

outsiders.name: swyx
outsiders.text: openai dot now has a setting to just solve all captchas for the rest of time https://t.co/rIqg7nVP8K https://t.co/3c2aTgvmUa

outsiders.name: clem 🤗
outsiders.text: As I’ve said for years, concentration of power, capabilities and wealth is the biggest risk in AI. The natural tendencies for it are super strong and without much much stronger open-source, we might end up in a world with more asymmetry and inequalities than ever! https://t.co/MXpSpPmaB6

outsiders.name: Amjad Masad
outsiders.text:
Technology is inherently recursively self-improving and the degree of autonomy has been going up overtime. AI is an accelerant but it didn’t not start this cycle.

Douglas Engelbart understood this. https://t.co/J3Zp1YNFXC

outsiders.name: Aravind Srinivas
outsiders.text: Teammates are awesome, and you can build them with any frontier model of your choice on Perplexity. No other product lets you do this. https://t.co/d5sNFVXVAt

outsiders.name: swyx
outsiders.text: also the day 1 livestream has crossed 100k in the fastest time ever. covering coding agent practices and landscape continues to be the strongest format we do and by far my strongest product-market-fit focus thing I have ever done. https://t.co/cM43xYQLMT https://t.co/Mr206bRvc7

virals.name: Elon Musk
virals.text: Text watermarking with Grok is only on where required by law or requested by the user https://t.co/GbSxfeRShc

virals.name: NVIDIA
virals.text:
AI is helping recyclers see more value in waste. ♻️

Discover how vision AI and robotics sort used clothing, bottles and mixed recyclables, recovering reusable materials and diverting thousands of tons from landfills.
